title: Why do we say "as mad as a hatter"? | IDIOM ORIGINS

entries.note: Covered in an earlier idiom episode; the popular theory linking it to a leg in a cast is just a satisfying pun, not the origin.
Originally clearing a path for others, as icebreaker ships do, recorded figuratively from 1590, before its literal use, probably translating the Latin [[from:scindere glaciem]].
The Latin idiom that English probably translated, which explains why [[gave:break the ice]] appears figuratively before literally.
From the flight envelope, an aircraft's operational limits, in test flying; popularised by Tom Wolfe's The Right Stuff with 'pushing the outside of the envelope'.
The air-filled part of a hot air balloon, which Rob briefly wonders might lie behind [[see:push the envelope]].
From World War II aviation: pushing ball-topped throttle grips forward to the cockpit [[see:firewall]] for maximum power or a dive.
The front wall of a cockpit protecting the pilot from engine fire, the wall in [[see:balls to the wall]].
Given as the equivalent of [[equivalent:balls to the wall]].
Another expression meaning the same as [[equivalent:balls to the wall]].
An older phrase meaning full speed, linked to the spinning balls of steam-engine governors, like [[see:balls out]].
From the weighted balls of a steam engine's centrifugal governor, which extend outward as it nears maximum speed.

entries.term: A Dialogue Containing the Number in Effect of All the Proverbs in the English Tongue
entries.note: A 1546 poem by [[see:John Heywood]] made almost entirely of idioms, nearly unreadable; a 1906 edition lists and explains them.
A lost 16th-century idiom from Heywood's book, similar to [[equivalent:head over heels]] or [[equivalent:ass over tit]].
Compared with the old idiom [[equivalent:tit over thumb]].
The modern phrase Rob compares with [[equivalent:tit over thumb]].

entries.term: folly it is to spurn against a prick
entries.note: Old idiom meaning don't push yourself against something pointy; to spurn against is to force yourself up against something.
Old idiom meaning to hit the bullseye, the [[see:prick]] being the point of the target.
Meant the target's point in [[see:ye shoot nigh the prick]]; people have punned on the word since at least Shakespeare.
Commonly traced to Hindus throwing ghee at statues of gods; the hosts prefer the idea of lavishing someone with valuable butter.

entries.term: it is not all butter that the cow shits
entries.note: A 15th–16th century idiom in Heywood's book, given there without a figurative explanation.

entries.term: sometimes a cigar is just a cigar
entries.note: Quoted to suggest [[see:butter someone up]] may simply mean using butter well.

entries.term: have your bread buttered on both sides
entries.note: To benefit from two conflicting parties at once, the opposite of [[see:there will be no butter cleave on my bread]].

entries.term: know which side your bread is buttered
entries.note: Found in Heywood's book and still used; meaning to know where your advantage comes from.

entries.term: there will be no butter cleave on my bread
entries.note: Old phrase meaning nothing to profit from, the inverse of [[see:have your bread buttered on both sides]].

entries.term: as sure as it were sealed with butter
entries.note: Old proverb meaning not secure at all, since a letter sealed with butter would soon come unstuck.

entries.term: I heard it through the grapevine
entries.note: Goes back to the unreliable 1859 [[from:grapevine telegraph]] line; famous from Marvin Gaye's song.
A Placerville–Virginia City wire slung over trees like vines, often broken; later used for Civil War camp gossip and enslaved people's covert networks.
Cheap springy wire for binding hay bales, used for makeshift repairs; going haywire comes via the [[from:haywire outfit]].
Probably from logging: a poorly equipped operation held together as if with haywire, linking the wire to modern [[gave:haywire]].
Predates [[see:Lewis Carroll]]'s Mad Hatter; hatters went mad from mercury poisoning by mercurous nitrate used in making felt hats.
Mad because hares are randy in March, which leads the hosts to [[see:hopping mad]].
Linked jokingly to the [[see:March Hare]] and possibly to [[see:mad as a box of frogs]].

entries.term: mad as a box of frogs
entries.note: Origin unknown, mainly British, fashionable in the 2000s; maybe from the hopping in [[see:hopping mad]].
Given as an example of a fashionable phrase, coming from the film Gaslight.
An 1980s band formed by ex-members of [[see:the Yardbirds]], clearly invoking [[see:mad as a box of frogs]].
British band that spawned Eric Clapton, Jeff Beck and Jimmy Page; former members formed [[see:Box of Frogs]].

entries.term: mad as a bag of cats
entries.note: A riff on [[see:mad as a box of frogs]]: anything that flails.
A 14th-century 'mad as' simile.
A 17th-century simile; the hosts can only speculate about plentiful spring milk or cows protecting their calves.

entries.term: as mad as a meat axe
entries.note: A simile recorded only in Australian and New Zealand usage.

entries.term: as mad as a cut snake
entries.note: An Australian simile that Rob says only Australia could produce.
Attested only in Derbyshire, meaning very angry; a [[see:tup]] is a ram.
Central English dialect for a ram; Jess guessed it from the 'tupping' line in Othello alongside [[see:the beast with two backs]].
Iago's line in Othello, which helped Jess guess the meaning of [[see:tup]].

entries.term: as mad as a wet hen
entries.note: The last 'mad as' simile Rob gives; hens are 'vicious little dinosaurs'.
No definitive origin; the popular theory of rivals stealing a racehorse's calming goat is doubted; compare French [[equivalent:to take the goat]].
An earlier French phrase meaning to make someone angry, perhaps by stealing their goat; a variant of [[equivalent:get someone's goat]].
One theory links it to [[see:get someone's goat]], though it doesn't really explain the phrase.
Discussed before as basically meaning goat preparer, showing how important goats were.
Discussed before as originally referring to property and cattle.
A costly, useless project or a gift exchange; from a Siamese king who gave fallen-from-favour courtiers sacred albino elephants that were ruinous to keep.
Hallucinations of late-stage alcoholism; seen in [[see:Pink Elephants on Parade]] and used in the [[see:Delirium]] brewery's logo.
The scary scene in Dumbo where the drunk Dumbo sees [[see:pink elephants]].
A famous Belgian brewery whose logo is a pink elephant.
Probably because someone withdrawing from drugs looks pale and clammy like a plucked turkey; popularised by Lennon's song [[see:Cold Turkey (song)]].
Rob's guess at the image behind [[see:cold turkey]], which Jess confirms.
John Lennon and Yoko Ono's song with the Plastic Ono Band, which helped popularise [[see:cold turkey]].
1920s slang for pleading guilty, perhaps related to [[see?:talking turkey]].
Speaking bluntly; said from the 1860s to come from a tale of a hunter trying to swindle a Native American out of a turkey.
Also big white chief; a deliberately clunky phrase mimicking and mocking Native American speech.
American, not Asian: warm autumn weather where Native Americans lived; 1812 and 1824 explanations both disparage Native Americans.
From the rising of [[from:Sirius]], the dog star; folk etymology links it to dogs suffering in the heat.
The dog star in [[see:Canis Major]], whose rising gives the [[see:dog days of summer]].
The constellation containing [[see:Sirius]].
From the 16th century: apprentices held candles over a master's work, so it means not even good enough to be the helper.
From pipe organs, whose stops control airflow; pulling them all out lets the organ play at full volume.
From testing gold, which resists nitric acid on a touchstone mark; dates to the 1700s and took off in the California Gold Rush.
Rob assumed it meant the same as [[see:acid test]].

entries.term: pull yourself up by your bootstraps
entries.note: Originally ironic, meaning an impossible feat, as in an 1888 physics school book; it now suggests something difficult but possible.
Using something smaller to lift something bigger, in entrepreneurship, computing and law; also a statistical method.
Pirates of the Caribbean character, an anachronism because bootstraps weren't common on boots until the 1870s.

entries.term: having your work cut out for you
entries.note: From 16th–17th century tailoring: assistants cut out the pieces, leaving the master the real work of assembling and stitching.
Means to cut, which would point toward [[see:having your work cut out for you]].
Origin uncertain; a satisfying theory links it to the well-dressed 99th Wiltshire Regiment.
From an old 0–10 cloud grading system, nine being very high but not the highest; the original was [[from:on cloud seven]].
The original form of [[gave:on cloud nine]].
Probably from the 19th-century North Carolina anecdote of the judge's big shirt; theories of ammunition belts, kilts and concrete trucks are less likely.
From the 1920s, pitting serious cash against cheap, zero-shaped donuts; preceded by [[see:dollars to buttons]] and [[see:dollars to dumplings]].
Rob's proposed British version of [[equivalent:dollars to donuts]], not actually in use.
An older expression contrasting cash with something trivial, like [[see:dollars to donuts]].
An older version of [[see:dollars to donuts]], dumplings being cheap.
Used, like donut, to mean zero in sport, supporting the zero theory of [[see:dollars to donuts]].
The same idea as [[see:dollars to donuts]], as Annie sings on Broadway.
From early Hollywood: cutting to the chase scene when audiences might be getting bored with the plot.
